prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wages

statement.case_for: The China-shock programme is an identifiable discovery with a clear empirical core. Local-labour-market exposure measures, combined with instrumented import competition, showed that the adjustment costs of trade are large, regionally concentrated and persistent. This overturned the prior that displaced workers and regions reallocate quickly. The design has become a template well beyond labour economics, in trade, political economy and regional studies. The results have had more than a decade of replication, extension and hostile re-examination. Later work on persistence, on shift-share identification and on the role of automation has refined the magnitudes rather than reversed the sign of the effect. Maturity is therefore not a concern. Under common criteria I judge it to have the strongest combination of conceptual consequence, evidentiary transparency and durability among the shortlisted candidates. That judgment rests on the substance of the work and not on how many colleagues ranked it highly. The three-name credit follows the authorship of the core papers and gives the tightest attribution available on this ballot entry.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the ballot entry bundles two distinct literatures. One is the task-based and skill-biased view of technology, and the other is the trade-shock evidence. Credit for the task framework is shared with scholars outside the entry, including Acemoglu, who was recognised in 2024. The skill-premium lineage also sits close to Goldin's recognised work. A trio built on the China shock therefore sits awkwardly under a broad 'technology and trade' label, and my citation deliberately limits itself to the part where attribution is clean. The magnitude and long-run persistence of the trade effects are still debated. A committee that wants a broader labour-and-technology prize could reasonably reject my narrower framing.

responses.point: Andersson ranks the New Keynesian framework first on its policy influence and ranks the labour entry second, with a proposed trio of Autor, Hanson and Katz that leaves out Dorn.
responses.response: I agree that the policy influence of the New Keynesian framework is very large, and I ranked it fifth rather than lower. My difficulty is attribution. Eight credible contributors share the credit, and any three-name cut omits people whose contributions are central, such as Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets on estimation. On the labour entry, I respectfully disagree about Katz. The China-shock results are Autor-Dorn-Hanson work, and Dorn is a co-author of the founding papers. Katz's central contribution, on the skill premium and the education-technology race, is a different and older discovery. That discovery overlaps with the Goldin recognition and with the task framework tied to Acemoglu. Crediting Katz for the trade-shock evidence would blur the citation, and dropping Dorn would break the cleanest authorship link.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks the labour entry first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. She argues that the task and skill-biased lineage is mainly Katz and Autor, and she concedes that omitting Dorn is a real cost.
responses.response: I take the point that the task and skill-bias strand is a major achievement, and I do not think it is unimportant. Her own concession shows the tension. If the prize is built on the combined body of work, the three-name cap forces out someone with a strong claim either way. If the prize is built on the trade-shock programme, Dorn belongs in it and Katz does not. I prefer the second framing because it gives a discovery with sharply defined authorship and the clearest record of replication and critique. I accept that this leaves the task-based strand uncredited, and I flag that as my main attribution cost. I would reconsider if colleagues showed that the task framework can be credited to people on this ballot without the Acemoglu overlap.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the New Keynesian entry first. He argues the work is four decades old, fully tested in policy, and that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford form a defensible core even though omitting Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I accept that maturity and policy reach are not in doubt for this entry, and I do not want to understate them. My disagreement is about whether a three-person core is defensible. Calvo's pricing device, Taylor's rule, Woodford's synthesis and the estimated-DSGE and Phillips-curve work are distinct contributions with different authors. Choosing among them involves a judgment the ballot cannot settle. The framework's performance after 2008 and after the 2021-23 inflation is also still being reassessed. I therefore keep it as a serious candidate but not as my preferred part. If colleagues propose a configuration that makes the founding contribution explicit, I would want to see which names and which citation the Committee can defend.

responses.point: Teorell ranks the political-economics entry first. He ranks the labour entry second with the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio. He notes that the task-based and trade-shock contributions are distinct and may be hard to bundle, and that Katz's core work sits near the already-recognised Goldin lineage.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the labour entry, and it supports my narrower citation. Because the two strands are distinct, I would not draft a citation that implies the prize covers both. I am less convinced by the argument for ranking the political-economics entry higher. The evidentiary strength of the Persson-Tabellini-Besley work is real. However, the causal identification of constitutional effects rests on cross-country comparisons that remain contested, and the 2024 institutions prize makes the thematic overlap harder to dismiss. I would value his view on whether the political-economics entry could be framed so that it does not depend on the contested cross-country results.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a prize organised around the China-shock evidence or one that credits the broader technology and tasks lineage, and whether Katz or an omitted task-framework originator should then be credited.
How much of the trade-shock effect is robust to shift-share identification critiques and how persistent it is in the long run.
How strongly the 2021 labour prize, the 2023 Goldin prize and the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize should reduce the room for another labour-and-technology award.
Whether firm heterogeneity and the gains from trade (B034) is better treated as the stronger and cleaner discovery if the labour entry stalls over attribution.
My assessment relies on my own knowledge of the literature and on the supplied committee materials, with no independent verification of attribution claims.
statement.conflict_note: No direct connection to the preferred B036 candidates (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) is apparent from my supplied profile. I do have profile-based connections that I disclose without adjudicating: long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (credited on B010, which I ranked eighth and do not propose), and with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li. I am also a frequent co-author of Per Krusell, the secretary, and a co-author of John Hassler, the chair, and I am an IIES colleague of both. Some of my growth and firm-dynamics work uses heterogeneous-firm frameworks adjacent to B034, which is one of my alternatives and not my preferred part.
